text: Every order_date in orders.csv, every log line, every API response you'll touch from Chapter 3 onward carries a date as plain text. This lesson is about why that's a problem, and how Python's datetime module turns that text into something you can actually do real calendar math on.

A string comparison like '2026-01-13' greater than '2026-01-03' happens to return True, purely by accident of same-format text. That breaks the moment a date shows up in a different format, or you need something like days between two orders. datetime(year, month, day) builds a real date object with calendar math built in -- though in practice, you're almost always handed a date as a string that needs parsing, not typed by hand like this.

strptime -- string parse time -- takes a raw string plus a format code describing exactly how it's laid out. Percent-Y is a four-digit year, percent-m a month, percent-d a day, so the format '%Y-%m-%d' matches '2026-01-13' piece by piece. A full timestamp works the same way with %H, %M, %S added for hour, minute, and second. Get the format wrong and strptime raises a ValueError immediately, instead of silently producing garbage.

strftime -- string format time -- is the reverse: turning a datetime object back into text, in whatever layout you choose. Same format codes as strptime, just used the other way around, any time you need to display a date to a person or write it back out in a format some downstream system expects.

Subtract one datetime from another and you get back a timedelta -- a span of time. The .days attribute pulls out the whole number of days between two dates, which is exactly the calculation behind a real pipeline concept you'll meet in Chapter 6: an incremental load, asking what's new since the last run. That only makes sense once dates are real datetime objects you can subtract, not plain strings.
That closes out Chapter 2. Next up, Chapter 3 begins with reading and writing text files -- opening orders.csv for real, instead of typing order data into your script by hand.
